stories.title: Liberia: WCO Delegates Adopt New Measures to Strengthen Intelligence-Sharing, Combat Cross-Border Crimes
stories.summary: Liberia: WCO Delegates Adopt New Measures to Strengthen Intelligence-Sharing, Combat Cross-Border Crimes 9 November 2026 Liberian Observer (Monrovia) By David a. Yates The 17th Joint Annual Meeting of National Correspondents of the World Customs Organization (WCO) Regional Intelligence Liaison Offices (RILO) for West and Central Africa has adopted a series of recommendations aimed at strengthening regional intelligence-sharing, improving customs enforcement and enhancing cooperation against cross-border crimes and illicit trafficking. The recommendations were adopted at the conclusion of the five-day meeting, held from November 2 to 6, 2026, at the Farmington Hotel in Margibi County, Liberia, under the theme, "Intelligence and Regional Cooperation in Support of Vigilant Customs Administrations Committed to Protecting Society." The meeting brought together National Correspondents, customs officials, regional intelligence representatives and other stakeholders from West and Central Africa to examine operational challenges, assess progress and identify measures to improve intelligence coordination among customs administrations. Among the key recommendations are stronger regional coordination, real-time intelligence-sharing, joint training and operations, improved national legal frameworks, increased institutional capacity and regular assessments of the effectiveness of intelligence activities. The poser is: after more than three decades, is an annual COP still the best way to advance the global climate agenda? The two-week conference opening on November 9 in Antalya will gather presidents, diplomats, scientists and activists to bring the climate emergency into sharp focus. Nearly 100 agenda items have been tabled for negotiations, ranging from climate finance and adaptation to loss and damage and energy transition. stories.title: Southern Africa: Southern African Farmers Prepare for Powerful El Nino With Agroecology
stories.summary: Southern African Farmers Prepare for Powerful El Nino With Agroecology Linda Mujuru/GPJ Agnes Tauzeni stands in her maize field in Mudzi, Zimbabwe, where repeated plantings have failed due to prolonged drought. 8 November 2026 Radio France Internationale By Farai Shawn Matiashe Farmer Dudzai Matsapa works under a scorching sun, digging small, shallow pits across his field in Nyanga, east of the Zimbabwean capital, Harare. He will later fill these potholes with organic manure and wait for the rainy season. This is all part of Matsapa's preparation for the anticipated El Nino, which is expected to trigger drought and extreme heat across southern Africa. "Instead of ploughing the entire land, I only disrupt the specific spot where plants will grow," Matsapa told RFI at his farm. The potholes technique - which captures water, concentrates organic matter and drastically improves crop yields in dry areas - is part of a practice known as agroecology, a system which produces food while protecting the environment. It involves sustainable farming practices that improve soil health, conserve water and increase biodiversity.

stories.title: At least 39 die after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders estimates that for every 100 people who reach the Canary Islands by sea, 21 die during the crossing (file photo) By Ondiro Oganga Â and Â Madina Maishanu ,Â BBC Africa Published 9 November 2026, 08:16 GMT Updated 30 minutes ago At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports. The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established. The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands. Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors. Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese.

stories.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, Paul Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", the judge said last month By Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Wycliffe Muia ,Â Reporting from Nairobi Published 6 November 2026 A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus". Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity. "The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added. The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.

stories.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Like many neighbouring countries, Guinea-Bissau waits until babies are six weeks old to vaccinate them against hepatitis B, while the WHO says it should be done at birth (file photo) By Basma El Atti Â and Â Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa Published 5 November 2026 A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial". The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy. The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns. Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.

Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed. “A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola ,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.” The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters. stories.summary: Publicité Récap Municipales en Afrique du Sud, JOJ Dakar 2026, Midterms pour l'Afrique : l'hebdo Afrique Publié le : 06/11/2026 - 13:50 6 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 Un homme vote lors des élections locales dans la commune d'Alexandra, à la périphérie de Johannesburg, en Afrique du Sud, le 4 novembre 2026. © Themba Hadebe, AP Les Sud-Africains se sont rendus aux urnes, mercredi, pour les élections municipales – dernière échéance électorale avant le scrutin général de 2029 –, au terme d'une campagne centrée sur la crise des services publics. Le maintien au pouvoir du président somalien Hassan Sheikh Mohamud est "illégal", car l'adoption d'une nouvelle Constitution en mars dernier, qui a prolongé de quatre à cinq ans le mandat présidentiel, ne pouvait s'appliquer à son mandat actuel, a tranché jeudi la Cour suprême somalienne. stories.title: Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated | Patience Akumu
stories.summary: Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu View image in fullscreen Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated Patience Akumu I wanted to be a beacon of black feminist love; my friends and family teased me for being a sellout W e had been together 20 years, had two children and had a customary marriage with our village sub-county two years ago without any real plans for a church wedding. So we called our second ceremony a celebration of love and not a wedding. How else would a self-professed African feminist survive being the centre of a colonial and Abrahamic religious ceremony that also manages to reinforce the most male-centred aspects of African culture? Our invitations came directly from me and my partner Mark, not – as is traditional – from our families, and in the form of a playful gif featuring the song Love Potion from the South African group Mafikizolo, a reminder that this was a wedding on our terms.
